submission.natural_language_explanation: Retrospective, position-gated token detector. The pole fires on the first token of a sequence whatever it is (all 59 distinct first tokens tested gave 0.06-0.41, including 'cat', '42', '--', 'Xylophone' and 'the') and is exactly 0 on the second token (22/22 pairs tested); from the third position on it fires (0.15-0.6) on a word-initial modifier/pronoun/conjunction token ('young', 'long', 'good', 'short', 'very', 'former', 'little', 'I', 'they', 'our', 'but') and stays at 0 on determiners, prepositions, copulas/auxiliaries and mid-word fragments ('the', 'of', 'in', 'on', 'be', 'was', 'is', '-tion'). Mechanically its pre-activation is 99% accounted for by the layer-0 attention output projected onto its key (r = 0.993 over 15,898 scanned tokens), so the same token can move several-fold with the preceding context; it prepares no particular upcoming token (zero-ablation KL = 8.8e-6, and its Jacobian-promoted tokens match none of the tokens that actually follow its peaks).

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Coastal shipping in the northern reaches has always depended on a fragile arrangement of charts, tides and luck. For most of the eighteenth century the harbour at Kestrel Bay kept no permanent light. Vessels arriving after dusk relied on the memory of local pilots, and the records of the period list a long sequence of groundings that the harbour board attributed to weather rather than to navigation. When the board finally petitioned for a lighthouse, the reply from the capital was cautious. Funds were short, the engineers were occupied elsewhere, and the merchants who stood to gain most from a light were unwilling to pay for one. The design that reached the board in the spring of 1804 was modest. A stone tower, thirty metres high, with a lantern room at the top and a keeper's cottage at the base. The estimate covered the tower, the lantern, the lamps, the oil store and a small pier for the supply boat. What the estimate did not cover was the road. The chosen site sat on a granite headland two kilometres from the nearest track, and every barrel of oil, every sack of coal and every length of timber would have to be carried up the slope by mule. Work began in July. The first season went well enough: the foundations were cut into the rock, the lower courses were laid, and the masons returned to the mainland before the autumn gales. The second season did not. A storm in February carried away the temporary pier, and a second storm in March undermined the western footing. The engineers rebuilt the footing with a wider base and a drainage channel, and the tower rose through the summer at a rate of about a metre a week. By the following spring the masonry was complete and the lantern had been fitted with seventeen lamps arranged on a circular frame. The light was first shown on the night of 3 October 1806. The keeper's log for that evening records a clear sky, a light breeze from the south-west, and a vessel standing off the bay at about four miles. The log does not record whether the vessel had been waiting for the light, but the harbour board later used the entry to argue that the tower had paid for itself within a single season. That claim was generous. Shipping traffic through the bay grew slowly for a decade, and the light was not fitted with a revolving lens until 1832, by which time the original lamps had been replaced twice and the keeper had been dismissed for reasons the surviving correspondence does not explain. What the record does show is how quickly the tower became ordinary. By mid-century the almanacs listed it without comment, the pilots stopped mentioning it in their depositions, and the harbour board's annual accounts carried the oil and the wages as a single line. A structure that had once required a petition, an estimate, two seasons of work and a debate in the capital had become part of the coastline, as unremarkable as the granite beneath it.
